summary: Budget 2026 adds $142 billion in new measures and keeps deficits above $50 billion a year, Ottawa says US trade talks are improving, and Ontario students walked out.
body: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled Budget 2026 on Thursday. It adds $142.1 billion in new measures over five years, partly paid for by stronger-than-expected revenue[^1][^2]. The deficit this year is $62.3 billion, about $3 billion less than forecast in the spring, and stays above $50 billion every year to 2030-31[^2][^6]. Debt stays near 40% of GDP, but interest on it costs $60.2 billion this year, more than Ottawa sends provinces for health care[^6][^2]. The biggest item is a business tax deduction meant to attract investment; there is also $3.5 billion for workers hurt by US tariffs, a one-time grocery benefit boost of up to $339 for a single person, and more defence spending[^3][^4][^5].

For students: the budget promises 175,000 youth work and skills placements in 2026-27 and a goal of up to 100,000 new Red Seal trades workers[^5]. Tuition and OSAP are provincial, and on Thursday students at more than a dozen Ontario campuses walked out over Ontario's cut to the grant share of student aid, from up to 85% to 25%, and tuition rises of up to 2% a year[^8]. The province says it is adding $6.4 billion for colleges and universities[^8].

Prime Minister Mark Carney says US negotiators have dropped demands on Canadian culture and on Canada's other trade deals: "They're asking less, and they're offering more, but we're not quite there"[^7]. The Liberals hold a majority, so the budget is expected to pass; Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has moved to reject it[^1]. October jobs figures come out this morning[^9].
differences: The government says its fiscal anchors are met: the operating budget balances a year early and debt-to-GDP is "broadly stable"[^1]. Poilievre calls it a "credit card budget"; economists from Desjardins and Queen's University warn that debt costs are rising and that the plan relies on optimistic revenue[^1][^2][^3]. The NDP says it favours corporations, and the Bloc says it costs Quebec revenue[^1].

reads.title: Carney's 'ambitious' but 'risky' budget eyes investment in uncertain world
reads.summary: A balanced look at Budget 2026's big bet on business investment, with economists on why it could work and why it is risky.
